section_summary: These pages trace Japanese activities in Brazil from a 1944 arson case through wartime propaganda investigations and, after Japan’s surrender, violence by groups that denied the defeat. FBI reports, consular despatches, cooperative appeals, a petition, and newspaper clippings describe intimidation of Japanese Brazilians who acknowledged the surrender, threats to agricultural production, and requests for reliable news and correspondence from Japan.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal concerning Hisashi Tamura
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits a report on Tamura’s confession to burning Japanese-owned cocoon barns in São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards a confidential-source memorandum on Tamura’s arson confession.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Hisashi Tamura’s confession
subfiles.about: Records Tamura’s account of setting fires at Japanese-owned silkworm cocoon barns.
subfiles.summary: A police source reports Tamura’s arrest and translated confession. Tamura describes persuasion by a Japanese tinker, preparation of timed incendiary hooks, and the burning of five barns on October 10, 1944.

subfiles.title: Division of Brazilian Affairs review of Japanese activities in Brazil
subfiles.about: Summarizes an embassy report on the Japanese population, suspected sabotage, and Brazilian controls.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes Japanese settlement, schools, agriculture, suspected espionage and crop sabotage, and propaganda in Brazil. It lists wartime restrictions on travel, language, schools, businesses, and coastal residence, concluding that police measures appear effective.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal on Kano, Iwata, and Muranaga
subfiles.about: Forwards a report on three Japanese residents convicted for clandestine propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends the State Department a report on propaganda convictions in São Paulo.

subfiles.title: Investigation of Isamu Kano, Massuni Iwata, and Mamoro Muranaga
subfiles.about: Details the arrests, backgrounds, propaganda charges, and sentences of three Japanese residents.
subfiles.summary: Police information identifies the three men and describes Japanese-language bulletins criticizing Brazilian policy. The Tribunal of National Security sentenced each to six months’ imprisonment.

subfiles.title: FBI notice of the Society of Veterans of the Japanese Empire in Brazil
subfiles.about: Reports São Paulo police raids on a society that refused to accept Japan’s surrender.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports the society’s aims, arrests, and seizure of propaganda and a directors’ list.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of Society of Veterans officials
subfiles.about: Forwards names of officials of the Japanese veterans’ society arrested in São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: Hoover encloses a memorandum naming society officials after police raids.

subfiles.title: Report on the Society of Veterans of the Japanese Empire in Brazil
subfiles.about: Describes the society’s objectives, rival groups, police raids, leaders, and publications.
subfiles.summary: Sources describe a society organized after the war that treated Japan’s surrender as unconfirmed and sought to discipline Japanese youth. The report compares it with other Japanese associations, describes police raids and seized publications, and lists society leaders with addresses. A source also alleges fundraising and misleading photographs circulated within the colony.

subfiles.title: Brazil Takes Stern Action
subfiles.from: Robert K. Shellaby, The Christian Science Monitor
subfiles.about: Reports Shindo Remmei violence and Brazilian responses to Japanese surrender denial.
subfiles.summary: The article describes intimidation, killings, arrests, fraudulent victory claims, and hostility toward Japanese immigration.

subfiles.title: Japanese in Brazil Formally Admit Nipponese Defeat
subfiles.about: Reports a manifesto in which Japanese societies acknowledge Japan’s defeat.
subfiles.summary: A signed manifesto accepts Japan’s defeat and urges Japanese communities to abandon contrary claims.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3886: Activities of Japanese Secret Societies in São Paulo
subfiles.about: Reports assassination threats against Japanese leaders who publicized Japan’s defeat.
subfiles.summary: Welch identifies eight threatened São Paulo residents and reports the murder of a cooperative figure. Japanese community leaders ask for censored family letters and newspapers from Japan to counter surrender denial. He forwards a lawyer’s memorial and recommends considering Shindo Remmei officers for repatriation.

subfiles.title: Secret letter on the Bastos murder and Shindo Remmei
subfiles.to: Paul C. Daniels, American chargé d’affaires
subfiles.about: Reports the murder of Ikuta Mizobe and threats to Japanese cooperative leaders.
subfiles.summary: Welch relays Piza’s account of Shindo Remmei’s intimidation, alleged production sabotage, and threats against Bastos cooperative leaders. He suggests repatriating society leaders and notes Piza’s planned meetings in Rio de Janeiro.

subfiles.title: Bastos cooperative appeal concerning Shindo Ketumei Dan
subfiles.from: Committee of interested members, Cooperativa Agricola de Bastos
subfiles.about: Seeks intervention against threats to Bastos farmers and cooperative leaders.
subfiles.summary: The committee alleges arson, death threats, anti-surrender propaganda, and efforts to force Mizobe from the cooperative. It asks Piza to keep him in office, seek São Paulo police action, and protect witnesses and agricultural production.

subfiles.title: Translation of the Bastos cooperative appeal
subfiles.from: Committee of interested members, Cooperativa Agricola de Bastos
subfiles.about: English translation of the cooperative’s request for protection from society threats.
subfiles.summary: The translation details threatened barn fires, denunciations of surrender believers, death warnings, and pressure on Mizobe. It names local society members and potential witnesses, and requests police protection and action against those disrupting the cooperative.

subfiles.title: Shindo Remmei officers, branches, and representatives
subfiles.about: Lists society officers and branch representatives across São Paulo and other Brazilian localities.
subfiles.summary: A roster names officers, branches, estimated membership figures, and local representatives.

subfiles.title: Memorial to Japanese citizens of Brazil
subfiles.about: Urges Japanese residents to accept the imperial surrender rescript and end violence.
subfiles.summary: The appeal recounts failed efforts to circulate official surrender news, rumors that the rescript was false, and intimidation of those who accepted defeat. It cites the Bastos murder, calls for an end to threats, and asks Japanese residents to obey Brazilian law while leaving crimes to the authorities.

subfiles.title: Telegram 90 on attacks and Japanese community requests
subfiles.about: Reports attacks on Furuya and Nomura and requests credible news from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The consul reports one death, a failed attack, and requests for letters, newspapers, official notices, films, and an emissary.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum on despatch 3907 and Franciscan letters
subfiles.from: Mr. Main, Division of Brazilian Affairs
subfiles.to: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests a decision on forwarding Franciscan letters to Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum sends despatch 3907 for action on two enclosed personal letters.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning personal mail to Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends holding the Franciscan letters pending a decision on personal mail to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Shaskan says personal mail service is under consideration and advises holding the letters.

subfiles.title: Instruction returning Franciscan letters
subfiles.to: American consular officer in charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Returns letters and explains current postal rules for Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: The Department returns two letters and describes restricted postcard service to Japan and reopened personal mail to Germany.

subfiles.title: Despatch 3907: Activities of Japanese Secret Societies in São Paulo
subfiles.from: Cecil M. P. Cross, American consul general
subfiles.about: Reports attacks on Furuya and Nomura and forwards a community petition and press clippings.
subfiles.summary: Cross reports the attempted killing of Furuya, Nomura’s murder, and altered surrender photographs used as propaganda. He renews requests for Japanese newspapers and repatriation of society leaders, and encloses the petition, clippings, and Franciscan letters.

subfiles.title: Petition from Japanese farmers and merchants in São Paulo
subfiles.from: Japanese agriculturalists and merchants in São Paulo
subfiles.about: Requests renewed correspondence and Japanese publications to counter false victory claims.
subfiles.summary: The petition describes confusion and conflict in isolated farming communities caused by false reports of Japan’s victory. Signatories seek controlled correspondence, newspapers, and magazines from Japan to establish the truth and protect agricultural work.

subfiles.title: Japanese Gestapo Organized in São Paulo
subfiles.about: Reports the killing of Ichuzaburo Nomura and attempted assassination of Shigetsuna Furuya.
subfiles.summary: The clipping describes shootings in São Paulo, arrests of two Japanese suspects, Nomura’s death, and an attack on former ambassador Furuya. It links the violence to fanatics who rejected Japan’s defeat. Pages 51–54 contain overlapping reproductions of the article.
